findings.source_passage: "... From an early age I realized that I had exceptional abilities. Only a fool underestimates his capabilities."
findings.source_locator: diary passage, early entries on self-assessment
findings.why_it_matters: The aphoristic rhythm 'Only a fool underestimates his capabilities' is a voice-defining line in the diary; the draft collapses the entry into a paraphrase that loses that rhetorical snap.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore the verbatim line 'Only a fool underestimates his capabilities' within the diary excerpt to preserve its distinctive self-serving logic.

findings.source_passage: "Then I studied the criminal in the dock.... The man was a fool--he had been incredibly, unbelievably stupid.... I felt an immeasurable contempt for him."
findings.why_it_matters: The murder-trial anecdote is the psychological origin-story of Mr. Brown's contempt for ordinary criminals and explains the logic of his double life; its complete absence removes a key interpretive beat.
findings.suggested_fix: Insert a compressed version of the murder-trial diary entry, preserving at minimum the contempt-for-the-criminal-in-the-dock beat.

findings.source_passage: "Degeneracy, disease--never the deliberate embracing of a career by a far-seeing man."
findings.source_locator: diary passage, after reading works on crime
findings.why_it_matters: This line is the rhetorical pivot of the diary—the distinction between degeneracy-crime and deliberate-career-crime is the intellectual core of Mr. Brown's self-justification and a key passage for any reading of the novel's villain.
findings.suggested_fix: Restore 'Degeneracy, disease—never the deliberate embracing of a career by a far-seeing man' as a direct quotation within the diary block.

findings.source_passage: "I have been reading a life of Napoleon. He and I have much in common...."
findings.why_it_matters: The Napoleon comparison is a classically Christie moment of grandiose villain self-assessment; its ironic economy is signature and it grounds the 'autocrat/dictator' dream in a culturally legible reference.
findings.suggested_fix: Add the single Napoleon line back into the diary excerpts.

findings.source_passage: "Morally, I shall always consider I have been jilted!"
findings.source_locator: Tuppence's exchange with Julius at the apartment door
findings.why_it_matters: This is the comic curtain line of the Julius-Tuppence sub-romance and a characteristically Tuppence-ian exit quip; though the scene is an authorized-cut subplot, the line's wit is the only payoff of the exchange.
findings.suggested_fix: The scene is inside authorized minor removal territory (Julius proposes subplot), so this is a low-severity note only; if any vestige of the exchange is retained, the closing line should come with it.

summary: The draft faithfully preserves Tommy's explanation and the diary's broad shape, but three medium-severity diary-passage losses—the murder-trial origin story, the 'degeneracy/disease' pivot line, and the 'only a fool underestimates' aphorism—strip the diary of its interpretive core and signature rhetoric, collectively triggering a regenerate verdict.
